pages.x: Fresh from building the Suez Canal, Ferdinand de Lesseps began digging across Panama, then part of Colombia, in 1881. He wanted a canal at sea level, as at Suez. But Panama had mountains, floods and jungle, and in 1889 his company went bankrupt, ruining thousands of French savers.

Most of the workers came from the Caribbean, many from Jamaica, and yellow fever and malaria killed them in their thousands. No one yet knew that mosquitoes carried them; hospital beds even stood in bowls of water to keep off ants, which bred more mosquitoes.
pages.of: died in the French years, by one estimate

pages.x: The United States wanted the canal for its navy and its trade. When Colombia refused its terms in 1903, President Theodore Roosevelt backed a revolt in Panama and sent warships to stop Colombian troops landing. Panama declared itself independent and within weeks gave the United States a strip of land across it.
The army doctor William Gorgas, who had seen in Cuba that mosquitoes spread yellow fever, drained swamps, screened windows, spread oil on standing water and fumigated houses.
pages.fx: Yellow fever was gone from Panama by 1906 and malaria sharply cut. Without that the canal could not have been built, and the same methods saved lives across the tropics.

pages.x: The American engineers gave up on a canal at sea level. They dammed the Chagres River to make Gatún Lake, then the biggest artificial lake in the world, and built giant locks to lift ships 26 metres up to it and down again on the far side.

The hardest part was cutting through the mountains at Culebra. Tens of thousands of workers, most from Barbados and other Caribbean islands, blasted rock and loaded it onto trains, while landslides kept burying their work. Black workers were paid in silver and white Americans in gold, and they lived apart.

The first ship passed through on 15 August 1914, but the First World War had just begun, and few noticed. The voyage from New York to San Francisco was cut by about 13,000 kilometres. Some 5,600 workers had died in the American years.

The canal made the United States a power in two oceans and became one of the busiest trade routes on earth. Panamanians resented the American zone that cut their country in two, and after years of protest the United States handed the canal to Panama on the last day of 1999.
